idiom_name: RSpec verifying double (instance_double) over the service class
implementation_notes: Plain doubles are not enough here, which is why rspec-mocks provides verifying doubles: instance_double('PriceService') fails if the stubbed method does not exist on the real class or is called with the wrong number of arguments, so the stand-in stays tied to the contract it replaces. When the service is HTTP, webmock stubs at the level of the HTTP client library (Net::HTTP and most popular gems), which keeps the tests unchanged when the production code switches libraries. A hand-written fake class is still the clearest option when the stand-in must implement behaviour instead of answering calls.
code_sketch:
prices = instance_double(PriceService, price: Money.new(9_99))

checkout = Checkout.new(prices)                 # injected collaborator
expect(checkout.total('A-1', 2)).to eq(Money.new(19_98))
expect(prices).to have_received(:price).with('A-1')

# wire-level alternative:
# stub_request(:get, 'https://prices.example/A-1').to_return(status: 200, body: '{"price":9.99}')
pitfalls: A plain double is a complete fiction: it answers methods the real class never had, which is exactly what verifying doubles exist to prevent - never use one for a remote contract.

WebMock disables real HTTP connections by default, so a test that forgets a stub fails with an unexpected-request error rather than silently reaching the network; background threads can interleave with the stubs.
Stubbing a method on the real class (a partial double) couples the test to the client's internals and hides the seam the pattern is supposed to make explicit.

variants.name: WebMock HTTP stubs at the client-library level
variants.implementation_notes: WebMock stubs HTTP requests at the level of the HTTP client library rather than at the object boundary, so there is no need to change tests when the production code changes HTTP library, and requests can be matched on method, URI, headers and body. Reach for it when the request the client builds is part of what the test must pin down.
variants.code_sketch:
stub_request(:get, 'https://prices.example/A-1').
  with(headers: { 'Authorization' => /Bearer .+/ }).
  to_return(status: 200, body: '{"price":9.99}',
            headers: { 'Content-Type' => 'application/json' })

expect(a_request(:get, 'https://prices.example/A-1')).to have_been_made.once
pitfalls: Unstubbed requests raise instead of hitting the network, so an unrelated URL added to the client breaks an unrelated test with a confusing error.
Matching on the full URI including query order is brittle; match the parts the contract actually specifies.
